questions.question: Explain why the plastic shopping bag became a serious environmental problem in South Africa, referring to its material, the three properties that cause the problem and the harms it causes.
questions.expected_answer: The bag is a thin film of high-density polythene, a few grams per bag, light, strong and almost free; about eight billion a year were used before 2003. Three properties combine: it is nearly free so it is discarded at once; it is very light so it blows out of bins and dumps and travels for kilometres; and it is not biodegradable so wherever it lands it persists. Harms: litter on fences and trees across the country (the 'national flower'), blocked storm-water drains causing flooding, pollution of rivers, beaches and the sea where turtles and seabirds swallow bags, livestock deaths from ingested plastic, growing microplastic pollution as bags fragment, and the cost of clean-up.

questions.question: Describe South Africa's 2003 Plastic Bag Regulations and evaluate their results, and explain the problems with biodegradable bags as an alternative.
questions.expected_answer: From May 2003 bags thinner than the set limit were banned (minimum 24 micrometres, so bags tear less, blow less and are reused), and shops had to charge for bags with a levy going to government to fund recycling. Results: bag use fell sharply at first (estimates up to 80 percent), litter on fences and in drains decreased and recycling of thicker bags became viable; but the small unchanged charge stopped deterring shoppers, use climbed back, the levy was not consistently spent on recycling, and thicker discarded bags contain more plastic, so total plastic may not have fallen. Biodegradable bags: starch bioplastics break down only in industrial composters, which South Africa largely lacks; oxo-degradable additives make bags fragment into microplastic; biodegradable bags contaminate polythene recycling. Woven reusable bags used many times are the most effective alternative; Kenya and Rwanda chose complete bans.

questions.question: Set out the structure of a case-study report and explain the difference between evidence and opinion, with an example of each.
questions.expected_answer: Title and introduction stating the question; background describing the product, material and use with figures; findings under headings presenting the evidence on harms, responses and results from both sides; discussion of what the findings mean, uncertainties and comparison of alternatives using life-cycle thinking; conclusion and recommendation that follow from the findings; sources. Optional table comparing bag types across source, manufacture, use and disposal, and a sketch or chart. Evidence is a checkable finding with a source, for example 'plastic bags blocked storm-water drains in Johannesburg and contributed to flooding'; opinion is an unsupported judgement such as 'plastic bags are terrible'. Numbers are given with source and date, and disagreements between sources are reported as ranges.
